docs.title: humanlike
docs.text:
Biomechanical human-likeness of simulated locomotion. humanlike compares the walking and running of physics-based controllers (reinforcement learning, motion imitation, behavior foundation models, muscle-driven models) with human locomotion. It does this through signatures of human motor control, not through positional error against a reference motion.

Signature What it asks Analysis Feedforward Do stride length and frequency scale with speed as in humans? Feedforward Feedback Does the next foot placement correct the pelvis state as in humans? Feedback Energetics Does the cost of transport have human-like walking and running optima? Energetics Joint kinematics Are the sagittal hip, knee and ankle angles human at the same speed? Sagittal angles Kinetics Do the ground reaction forces and joint work follow the principles of human walking? Kinetic principles Phases of the stride Double support, single support and flight Gait phases

The analyses that run depend on what the data contain. Positions of the pelvis and the feet are enough for the feedforward and feedback signatures. Joint torques add energetics, foot ground reaction forces add the kinetics and the phases of the stride, and sagittal joint angles add the joint kinematics.

docs.title: Ways to use it
docs.text:
• In the browser: the web app runs every analysis on your files (Minari datasets, C3D, BVH, CSV) without installing anything. The data stay on your computer.
  • From the command line: humanlike inspect, humanlike evaluate and an HTML report (Quick start).
  • From a running simulation: record a policy under a standard protocol in MuJoCo/Gymnasium or Isaac Lab, and evaluate it in one call (RL integration).

Every analysis reports how much data it had to work with (speeds, rollouts, strides), marks values that rest on too little data, and gives bootstrap intervals (Data coverage and uncertainty).

The human reference data are from Camargo et al. (2021), A comprehensive, open-source dataset of lower limb biomechanics in multiple conditions of stairs, ramps, and level-ground ambulation and transitions, Journal of Biomechanics 119:110320 (CC BY 4.0). See Reference data.

docs.title: Citing
docs.text:
If you use humanlike, please cite the accompanying paper (reference to follow on publication) and the human reference data:

Camargo, J., Ramanathan, A., Flanagan, W., & Young, A. (2021). A comprehensive, open-source dataset of lower limb biomechanics in multiple conditions of stairs, ramps, and level-ground ambulation and transitions. Journal of Biomechanics, 119, 110320.

Code: Apache-2.0. Derived reference data and results: CC BY 4.0.

docs.title: Installation
docs.text:
humanlike needs Python 3.10 or newer.

pip install "humanlike[minari]"        # analyses + Minari datasets
pip install "humanlike[rl]"            # + recording policies in MuJoCo / Gymnasium (gymnasium, mujoco)
pip install "humanlike[figures]"       # + matplotlib, for figures from the results

Until the release on PyPI, install from the source tree:

git clone https://github.com/jlee52/humanlike-eval
cd humanlike-eval
pip install -e ".[minari]"

The reference data (references/v1, the human data each analysis compares with) ship with the source tree. When the package is installed elsewhere, point HUMANLIKE_REFERENCES at that directory.

Isaac Lab has its own Python installation. Install humanlike into it with pip install -e . from the source tree. Isaac Sim's numpy 1.26 is supported.

Optional readers. C3D files need pip install ezc3d. Arrow-format Minari datasets need pip install "minari[arrow]"; HDF5 is read and written with h5py alone.

docs.title: 1. Look at the data
docs.text:
humanlike inspect my-controller-v0

inspect takes a Minari dataset with the humanlike profile (a directory or a registered id). It shows, without running the analyses:

  • the rollouts, falls, and commanded and measured speeds;
  • the sampling rate, the signals, and where the foot strikes come from;
  • for each analysis, whether the speeds, rollouts and strides meet its minimum and recommended coverage.

Data in other formats are converted first (Adapters):

humanlike convert c3d trial.c3d humanlike/subject01-v0 --name "Subject 01" --mass 70 --treadmill-speed auto

docs.title: 2. Evaluate
docs.text:
humanlike evaluate my-controller-v0 -o results/

This writes results/results.json (every number, with intervals and data coverage) and results/report.html (a self-contained report). An analysis whose signals are missing, or whose data are too few, is listed with the reason. A stage cache (~/.cache/humanlike) makes repeated runs fast.

humanlike summarize results/results.json prints the headline number of each analysis: one row, as on the leaderboard, with no combined score.

docs.title: 3. In Python
docs.text:
from humanlike.format import load
from humanlike.engine import evaluate

ds = load("my-controller-v0")
res = evaluate(ds)                       # bootstrap=200, coverage="enforce" by default
res["stages"]["gait_scaling"]["result"]["camargo-treadmill/gait"]["js_stride_length"]

Data sets can also be built from arrays (humanlike.adapters.from_arrays) or recorded from a running simulation (RL integration).

docs.title: 4. Or in the browser
docs.text: The web app does all of this in the browser: drop a Minari dataset, C3D, BVH or CSV file, map the columns if needed, and read the report.

docs.title: Recording and evaluating RL policies (humanlike.rl)
docs.text: pip install -e ".[rl]" (gymnasium, mujoco; .[minari] adds the official minari package).

docs.title: MuJoCo / Gymnasium environments
docs.text:
from humanlike.rl import HumanlikeRecorder
env = HumanlikeRecorder(make_env(), body_map="humenv-smpl")
obs, info = env.reset(options={"humanlike": {"group": "1.10", "commanded_speed": 1.1, "skip_s": 10}})
while True:
    obs, rew, terminated, truncated, info = env.step(policy(obs))   # info["humanlike"]: this step's samples
    if terminated or truncated:
        break
ds = env.dataset("MyPolicy")       # humanlike.engine.evaluate(ds), or saved as a Minari dataset

The recorder samples after every physics step, not every env step: while the wrapped env steps, mujoco.mj_step is intercepted for this env's MjData and run one step at a time. The trajectory is unchanged (tests/test_rl.py) and the samples are the profile signals (PROFILE.md):

signal from pelvis, left/right foot position xpos of the body map's bodies left/right ground reaction force contact forces between the floor and each foot's bodies (mj_contactForce, world frame, force on the foot) centre of mass position, velocity subtree_com, subtree_linvel of the root joint torque, velocity qfrc_actuator, qvel of every DOF except the free root sagittal angle, moment, power the body map's hip, knee, ankle (deg, N m, W; sign per the body map)

The number of physics steps per env step (k) is read from frame_skip or given as physics_steps=; it must be constant. Episodes whose pelvis drops below fell_height (0.5 m), or that end by termination, are marked as falls. An environment that steps without mujoco.mj_step (bound by name at import, or stepped in compiled code) raises an error at the first step; allow_env_rate=True records one sample per env step instead (too coarse for the GRF analyses below ~100 Hz).

Body map. Where the pelvis, feet and sagittal joints are: a preset (humenv-smpl, myoleg) or BodyMap(pelvis, left_foot, right_foot, sagittal={"hip": (joint, sign), ...}, side, leg_length_m). The sign makes flexion positive at the hip and knee and dorsiflexion positive at the ankle. The floor is a geom name, several names (terrain of several geoms), or "world" (every geom not part of the robot).

Check the recording first. env.check() tests a finished episode (humanlike.rl.checks); evaluate_policy does this after the first episode that did not fall and stops on a failure:

check fails when horizontal GRF the pelvis travels (≥ 0.3 m/s) but the largest horizontal floor force is < 3 % of body weight (normal forces only, no friction), or the mean horizontal force differs from m Δv / T by > 2 % of body weight force vs COM accel. at every sample the floor force should equal m (a_COM + g): per axis slope outside 0.9–1.1 or r < 0.8 (wrong force scale, missed contacts) sample rate below 100 Hz (physics steps not captured) vertical GRF Fz below -2 % of body weight (force of the foot on the floor, or z not up) impulse balance mean vertical floor force differs from m (g + Δv_z / T) by more than 10 % (missed floor contacts) unlisted contacts the feet touch geoms outside the robot that are not the floor (terrain missing from floor) non-foot contacts other bodies carry ≥ 5 % of the vertical floor force (a foot segment missing from the feet) feet below pelvis median pelvis height above the feet < 0.3 leg lengths (wrong bodies or up axis) joint axes (MuJoCo) a sagittal joint does not turn about the mediolateral axis L = z × forward (|axis · L| < 0.5: an abduction or rotation joint), or its sign disagrees with the direction of the turn (hip flexion and ankle dorsiflexion turn about −L, knee flexion about +L) segment rotation the recorded angle does not follow the rotation of the distal segment relative to the proximal one (pelvis–thigh, thigh–shank, shank–foot) about the same axes: r < 0.5 (r ≤ −0.5: flipped sign), or slope outside 0.3–3 (radians vs degrees) knee sign, hip sign only without segment orientations: median knee < −5 deg, median hip < −15 deg (gross errors only)

Forward is where the feet point (MuJoCo), else where the pelvis travelled. On the BFM-TS rollout the signs pass (segment rotation r = 0.86, 0.80, 0.79) and flipping any one of hip, knee or ankle fails both sign checks.

Minari. minari_io.collector(env) records the same infos with a Minari DataCollector, and minari_io.finish(collector, "org/name-v0", episodes=env.episode_metadata(), **env.profile_metadata()) writes the dataset with the profile metadata.

docs.title: Evaluation protocol
docs.text:
from humanlike.rl import evaluate_policy
out = evaluate_policy(make_env, policy, "humenv-smpl", "locomotion-speed-v1")
out["results"]; out["dataset"]

make_env(speed) returns an environment commanded to move at speed m/s; policy(obs) returns an action (a reset() method is called at every episode). The protocol fixes what makes models comparable:

protocol speeds (m/s) rollouts per speed duration left out locomotion-speed-v1 0.5-4.3, step 0.2 20 20 s first 10 s locomotion-speed-walk-v1 0.5-1.9, step 0.2 20 20 s first 10 s locomotion-speed-quick-v1 0.7, 1.1, 1.5 3 15 s first 5 s (development only)

locomotion-speed-v1 is the protocol of the manuscript's rollouts.

The protocols are for level ground. The analyses and the human references assume it: z is up, the floor is horizontal, speeds come from the horizontal pelvis motion, and gait events, vertical forces and the pendular energy exchange are read against gravity. Slopes, stairs and uneven terrain are outside the protocols, and the recording checks fail a steady climb or descent ("level ground").

humanlike validate DATA --protocol locomotion-speed-v1 (humanlike.rl.conformance) checks that a data set was recorded under a protocol, as the leaderboard does for a submission: every commanded speed with its rollouts (a fallen rollout counts towards its speed and may be shorter; the falls are reported), the duration of the others within one 30 Hz step, the transient left out, sampling at >= 100 Hz, and the recording checks on one rollout at the slowest, middle and fastest speed. humanlike summarize results.json gives the leaderboard row (humanlike.summary): the headline number of each analysis against the public human reference, never combined into one score.

docs.title: Memory, provenance and a first look
docs.text:
Memory - A protocol at the physics rate is large: 400 rollouts of 20 s at 500 Hz with the torques of a 23-joint humanoid take ~3 GB in float64. - Both recorders take three options (humanlike.rl.storage), applied when an episode ends: - dtype="float32" halves the memory. - keep_transient=False drops the start-up transient while recording, half again for the protocols. The rollouts record it as transient_dropped_s, which the protocol conformance counts. - spill_dir= writes each episode to .npy files and keeps memory-mapped views only. - evaluate_policy(..., recorder_kw={"dtype": "float32", "keep_transient": False}) passes them on. - rec.memory_bytes() reports what the finished episodes hold in memory.

Provenance. evaluate_policy stores what produced the data in the dataset metadata (dataset.provenance), and it is kept in the Minari profile metadata: - the protocol and the seed (episode i uses seed + i); - the body map and the recording options; - the versions of humanlike, Python, NumPy and the simulator packages; - the names of make_env and the policy; - the time of recording.

It is enough to rerun the protocol with the same code; it does not replace the policy's own checkpoint and configuration.

humanlike inspect DATA gives a quick overview without running the analyses: - the rollouts, falls, commanded and measured speeds; - the sampling rate and the transient; - the signals, the foot-strike source and the provenance; - for each analysis, whether the data's speeds, rollouts and strides meet its minimum and recommended coverage (docs/oss/COVERAGE.md).

Examples. examples/: a Gymnasium MuJoCo environment, and pointers to the humenv and Isaac Lab checks.

docs.title: MyoLeg (KINESIS)
docs.text:
The myoleg body map was checked on the manuscript's KINESIS rollouts (scripts/check_rl_myoleg.py): the physics-rate logs replayed state by state through the recorder's extractor reproduce the logged ground reaction forces, and every recording check passes after the start-up. The check covers joint axes +1 for hip, knee and ankle, and segment rotation r 0.98–1.00. The feet calcn + toes carry the whole floor force.

During its first ~3 s KINESIS stands and turns. Joint axes averaged over that part, against the first sample's forward direction, do not match the gait. This is why check() leaves out each episode's skip_s.

docs.title: Isaac Lab
docs.text:
from humanlike.rl.isaaclab import IsaacLabRecorder, add_foot_contact_sensors
add_foot_contact_sensors(env_cfg, body_map)          # before gym.make: one ground-filtered sensor per foot body
env = gym.make(task, cfg=env_cfg)
rec = IsaacLabRecorder(env, body_map)
for _ in range(n):
    obs, rew, terminated, truncated, info = env.step(policy(obs))
    rec.after_step(terminated, truncated)
rec.close(); ds = rec.dataset("MyPolicy")

The recorder wraps scene.update (called after every physics step) and samples all environments: body_pos_w, the foot GRFs, the mass-weighted body centres of mass, the joint torques (below), joint_vel, joint_pos.

Ground reaction forces need the foot sensors. An Isaac Lab contact sensor's net_forces_w sums the normal contact forces only, so the scene's usual contact_forces sensor gives no braking or propulsive force (in the H1 velocity task its horizontal component is ~1e-5 N). add_foot_contact_sensors adds one sensor per foot body, filtered to the ground (Isaac Lab reports filtered contacts only for a sensor on a single body); the recorder adds their normal forces (force_matrix_w) and friction forces (friction_forces_w where Isaac Lab has track_friction_forces, else the PhysX contact view's get_friction_data, e.g. Isaac Lab 2.3). Without these sensors the recorder falls back to net_forces_w, warns and labels the data set (grf_source), and check() fails on walking data. The ground defaults to the flat terrain's collision plane; pass ground= for other terrain.

rec.check() runs the checks above (without the contact checks only MuJoCo can make, and without the joint-axis check). For the segment-rotation check give the body map's segments (pelvis, thigh, shank and foot bodies); their body_quat_w is sampled at ~50 Hz for the check only.

Joint torques of implicit actuators come from PhysX. With implicit actuators (ImplicitActuator, PD gains handed to PhysX; the default of many Isaac Lab humanoids, H1 among them), applied_torque is Isaac Lab's evaluation of the PD law on the state before the step. PhysX applies the drive implicitly, so that is not the effort it applies.

The recorder takes the drive torque from PhysX instead (joint_torque="auto"): the joint force PhysX transmits along each DOF (root_physx_view.get_dof_projected_joint_forces()) plus the joint armature times the DOF acceleration. The armature (a rotor inertia) is needed because PhysX's mass matrix leaves it out.

scripts/check_isaaclab_torques.py established this on the H1 task with its published policy:

Test Reference Result pelvis fixed in the air, explicit actuators the applied torque M·q̈ + c + g from PhysX's own dynamics terms, plus armature·q̈, reproduces it away from joint limits: R² ≥ 0.997, summed |power| within 0.03 % walking, explicit actuators the applied torque projected joint force + armature·q̈: R² 0.998–0.9999 per joint group, |power| within 0.1 % walking, implicit actuators projected joint force + armature·q̈ applied_torque is off by +4.9 % in summed |power| (knee R² 0.996); the PD law on the post-step state by −0.9 % (ankle R² 0.84)

Caveats - At a joint limit the transmitted force also holds the passive limit force. There (within 0.01 rad of a limit) the recorder uses applied_torque, and check() reports the share of such samples ("joint limits": fails above 5 %). - joint_torque="applied" keeps the old behaviour; "physx" uses the PhysX torque for explicit actuators too. - Without the PhysX articulation view the recorder falls back to applied_torque and warns.

The package runs with Isaac Sim's numpy (1.26) as well as numpy 2.

docs.title: Validation
docs.text: MuJoCo recorder vs the manuscript's BFM-TS rollouts identical to float32 precision (relative difference < 1e-7) for GRF, COM, torques, velocities, positions; k = 15, 450 Hz; passes every check, and each flipped sagittal sign fails (scripts/check_rl_recorder_bfm.py) checks each failure produced on purpose (wrong foot body, terrain geom missing from the floor, flipped knee, uncaptured physics steps) in tests/test_rl.py trajectory unchanged by recording, GRF = body weight when standing, Minari round trip, protocol tests/test_rl.py (small MuJoCo model) Isaac Lab recorder Isaac Lab 2.3 / Isaac Sim 5.1, H1 velocity task with its published policy at 1 m/s, GPU and CPU (scripts/check_rl_recorder_isaaclab.py): every check passes (force vs COM acceleration slope 1.00, r 0.95-0.99 per axis; segment rotation r 1.00), each flipped sagittal sign fails, the normal-only fallback fails the horizontal-GRF and force checks; the engine runs on the recording (the kinetic stage skips: the policy's contacts last ~0.09 s, below the 0.10 s a strike needs) Isaac Lab recorder, interface against an object with Isaac Lab's interface (tests/test_rl.py) myoleg preset bodies, joints and floor found in KINESIS's myolegs.xml; joint axes give the preset's signs (+1, +1, +1); not yet run in a rollout

docs.title: Protocols and the leaderboard
docs.text:
Results of different controllers are comparable only when they were recorded the same way. A protocol fixes: - the commanded speeds; - the rollouts per speed and their duration; - the start-up transient left out.

Protocol Speeds (m/s) Rollouts per speed Duration Left out locomotion-speed-v1 0.5–4.3, step 0.2 20 20 s first 10 s locomotion-speed-walk-v1 0.5–1.9, step 0.2 20 20 s first 10 s locomotion-speed-quick-v1 0.7, 1.1, 1.5 3 15 s first 5 s (development only)

humanlike.rl.evaluate_policy records a policy under a protocol (RL integration). The protocols are for level ground.

docs.title: Checking a recording
docs.text:
humanlike validate my-controller-v0 --protocol locomotion-speed-v1 --json validation.json

The check confirms: - every commanded speed, with its rollouts (falls count, and are reported); - the duration of the rollouts that did not fall, within one 30 Hz step; - the transient left out; - sampling at the physics rate (≥ 100 Hz); - the recording checks on one rollout at the slowest, middle and fastest speed: ground reaction forces, the body map, joint signs and level ground.

docs.title: The leaderboard row
docs.text:
humanlike evaluate my-controller-v0 -o results/
humanlike summarize results/results.json -o row.json

The row holds the headline number of each analysis against the public human reference, side by side, with its bootstrap interval and data coverage. There is no combined score: the analyses measure different things, and a data set without a signal has no value for the analyses that need it.

The public leaderboard, with submissions as pull requests and data hosted on the Hugging Face Hub, opens with the publication of the accompanying paper.

docs.title: Analyses
docs.text:
humanlike evaluate runs every analysis the data support, in dependency order. Each stage reports ok, skipped (with the reason: a missing signal, or too little data) or error.

Stage Needs Compares with Headline numbers events pelvis and foot positions (or foot GRF) — foot strikes of each foot (Foot strikes) gait_summary core — speed, stride length and frequency per rollout gait_scaling core human speed–stride relations JS divergence; robust z at matched speed (Feedforward) foot_placement, feedback core human foot-placement fits FPGD; peak ΔR² and its timing (Feedback) energetics joint torques and velocities, body mass criteria of the human speed–COT profile PASS / FAIL with the first criterion failed (Energetics) gait_phases foot GRF, body mass — double support, single support, flight (Gait phases) sagittal sagittal joint angles human angles at the same speed features within the human range, shape distance (Sagittal angles) kinetic_principles foot GRF, body mass (+ sagittal moments for the joint-work predictions) human treadmill kinetics predictions consistent with human walking, of 16 (Kinetic principles)

Core signals are the pelvis and both feet's positions. The profile defines all signals and the metadata.

docs.title: Common definitions
docs.text:
• Strides run from one foot strike of the reference foot to its next.
  • Walking direction of a stride: the horizontal pelvis displacement over the stride.
  • Stride length: the horizontal displacement of the reference foot, projected on the walking direction.
  • Speed: the mean horizontal pelvis speed over the stride.
  • Stride frequency: speed / stride length.
  • Gait cycle: both strikes included, resampled to 101 points.
  • A rollout is summarized by the mean over its strides after its start-up transient (skip_s).
  • Rollouts that fell are left out.

These definitions are the same for every data set, simulated or captured.

Speed matching. Human values depend on speed, so a model's value is compared with the human median and spread at the same speed. The human distribution is fitted by quadratic quantile regression of the subject means on speed. The robust z is (value − median) / (IQR / 1.349), and a model is within the human range when |median z| ≤ 2.

Uncertainty and coverage. Every summary value has a 95 % bootstrap interval. Each analysis also declares the data it needs (speeds, rollouts, strides) and reports whether the data meet it (Data coverage and uncertainty).

docs.title: How much data each analysis needs
docs.text:
reports/coverage_sensitivity.py subsamples the manuscript's rollouts. The full design is 20 commanded speeds × 20 rollouts (KINESIS: 10 speeds). Each draw keeps either k random commanded speeds (with all their rollouts) or r random rollouts at every speed. Each analysis is then recomputed exactly as reported. The full-data values reproduce the manuscript: sagittal 2/3/7/1/2, principles 7/10/10/5/10, AMP FPGD 180.9, and the foot-placement refits are identical to the curated fits.

The study used 200 draws per level (50 for the principles and 20 for the foot-placement refits). The output files are in reports/output/coverage/: summary.csv, ranking.csv and draws.csv.

docs.title: Findings (2026-10-25)
docs.text:
Analysis Speeds needed Rollouts per speed What goes wrong below JS stride length / frequency ≥ 6 in the reference range (≤ 10 % from full for every model) 1–2 suffice (≤ 16 %) The speed distribution enters the joint KDE. With 1 speed, AMP is 75 % off. The ranking of close models (BFM-TS 0.80, KINESIS 0.82) needs every speed. BFM-TA is at the 1-bit ceiling. FPGD 1–4 (≤ 10 %; groups are scored independently) ≥ 10 (≈ 100 strides per group fit) Biased upward with few strides. At r = 2: AMP 231 vs 181, KINESIS 384 vs 318, SMP 205 vs 185. Small submissions look less human-like. AMP vs SMP (2 % apart) cannot be ranked from any subsample. Peak ΔR² BFM: 12 speeds still 6–13 % off ≥ 5–10 Depends on which speeds are included (strongly for BFM): the mean over speed groups mixes speeds. CoT verdict the full range, walking and running (≥ 12) ≥ 10 Spurious PASS. With 4 speeds, AMP gets PASS in 68 % of draws (all models FAIL with full data). With 1 speed the fit fails and is labelled FAIL (should be "not evaluable"). Sagittal (features with |median z| ≤ 2) ≥ 4 for ±1 feature ≥ 3 for ±1 Exact counts flip near the threshold (AMP ankle median z −2.05). At r = 10, AMP agrees in 57 % of draws and KINESIS in 78 %. Kinetic principles ≥ 3 spanning ≥ 0.6 m/s for all 16 to be evaluable; ≥ 6 for ±1 ≥ 3–5 (AMP 10) for ±1 With 1 speed only 10 of 16 are evaluable, so the counts drop. Exact counts are threshold-sensitive. Gait phases (walking) any speed with strides at 0.9–1.5 m/s 1 Not evaluable when no stride falls at walking speeds (BFM with 1 random speed: 78 %). SMP's double support is near 0, so its relative error is large but its absolute error is small.

Overall pattern - Speed coverage decides the speed-relation analyses: JS, CoT and the principles. - Strides per group decide the fitted analyses: FPGD, peak ΔR² and CoT. - Threshold counts (sagittal, principles) are unstable near their thresholds whatever the sample size.

Caveats - The study subsamples five models only. - Speeds are drawn at random, not as contiguous ranges. - The full-data values have their own sampling error. - Levels above the number of eligible speeds equal the full data.

docs.title: Minimum and recommended data (implemented: humanlike/coverage.py)
docs.text:
Analysis Minimum (else "not evaluable") Recommended (else flagged "low") Feedforward JS 3 speed levels in the reference range 6 levels Feedback (FPGD, peak ΔR²) median 100 strides per group 250 strides per group Energetics (CoT) speeds from ≤ 1.0 to ≥ 3.0 m/s, 8 levels 12 levels, 10 rollouts per level Sagittal none (compared at matched speed) 4 levels, 20 rollouts Kinetic principles none (direction and shape: 0.6 m/s span, n/a below) 6 levels, 5 rollouts per level

Speed levels - A speed level is the commanded speed when every rollout has one. - Otherwise it is the measured speed to the nearest 0.2 m/s. - The CoT's range comes from the commanded speeds. A model that was commanded to run and cannot is evaluated and fails; it is not excused.

Where it shows - Every gated stage result carries coverage (ok, low or insufficient, with what is missing). - A stage skipped for coverage gives the reason. - evaluate(..., coverage="report") computes the analysis anyway, flagged. - The HTML report shows a "Data coverage" column, and the web app notes the low-coverage analyses. - The leaderboard row (humanlike summarize) has coverage. The leaderboard page marks low values with † and the analyses that are not evaluable with n/e.

The manuscript models meet every minimum except KINESIS for the CoT. KINESIS was commanded to 0.5–2.3 m/s only, so its walk–run test is not evaluable. The manuscript reports FAIL; the manuscript pipeline does not apply these rules.

In the study's counts, BFM-TS reaches only 5 speed levels inside the human range of the kinetic principles, so it would be flagged low there.

docs.title: Uncertainty and the speed-matched comparison (implemented)
docs.text:
Bootstrap intervals (humanlike/bootstrap.py) - Every summary value carries a 95 % interval. Rollouts (or groups, for the feedback signature) are resampled 200 times with a fixed seed, so the results repeat. evaluate(..., bootstrap=0) leaves them out. - The intervals cover: - JS; - FPGD and the peak ΔR² mean; - the median z of every sagittal feature and kinetic magnitude prediction; - the count of consistent sagittal features (AMP: 6, interval 5–7, because the ankle sits at z = −2.05); - double support and the flight share. - The COT gets label_stability, the share of resamples with the same verdict (resampled within speed levels). - An interval shows how much a value would move with another draw of the same design. It does not cover a biased design: that is what the coverage rules are for.

Stride length and frequency at matched speed - Each rollout gets a robust z against the human median and spread at its own speed (SpeedModel, as the sagittal and kinetic analyses). The result is the median z, its interval, |z| ≤ 2, and a per-speed profile (by_speed). - Unlike JS, z does not mix in which speeds the data cover, and it does not saturate. BFM-TA's JS is 1.0 bit, the maximum, but its z separates it: stride length −9.9, frequency +19.9, against AMP −1.2 and +1.5. - z still summarises only the speeds covered. A model whose deviation changes with speed gives a different median for different speed sets. In the subsampling, BFM-TA moves by 1–2 z for length and 5–10 z for frequency, while AMP moves by less than 0.5 and its verdict never flips. That movement is a property of the model, not noise, so the profile is reported alongside the median. - No speed-matched form of peak ΔR² is possible yet. The feedback reference (21 subjects walking overground at self-selected speed) has no speeds; it would need foot-placement fits per subject and speed, for example from the treadmill trials.

docs.title: Energetic signature: cost of transport
docs.text:
Human walking and running each have an energetically optimal speed. The cost of moving away from these optima shapes how humans choose their speed and gait.

Mechanical cost of transport per rollout, after the transient:

COT = Σₜ Σⱼ |τⱼ(t) ωⱼ(t)| Δt / (m g d)

The sum runs over the actuated joints and every sample. τ and ω are the joint torques and velocities, m the body mass, and d the distance the pelvis travelled. It counts the mechanical work of the actuators: a proxy for metabolic cost, not an estimate of it.

Two-Gaussian profile. The z-scored COT against speed is fitted with

y(v) = c + a₁ exp(−(v − μ₁)² / 2σ₁²) + a₂ exp(−(v − μ₂)² / 2σ₂²)

The fit uses bounded soft-L1 least squares, with the walking optimum μ₁ in 0.5–2.0 m/s, the running optimum μ₂ in 2.2–4.0 m/s, and the widths in 0.05–0.6 m/s. The profile is human-like (PASS) only if all of the following hold, checked in this order; the first that fails is reported:

  1. random residuals: Durbin–Watson 1.5–2.5 and Wald–Wolfowitz runs test p ≥ 0.05;
  2. adequate fit: R² ≥ 0.60 and RMSE ≤ 0.80;
  3. two pronounced valleys: a₁, a₂ ≤ −0.5 and |a₁|, |a₂| ≤ 10;
  4. non-overlapping valleys: σ₁ + σ₂ ≤ μ₂ − μ₁;
  5. distinct optima: μ₂ − μ₁ ≥ 1.2 m/s.
Output Meaning speed, cot per rollout fit the fitted parameters and the fit statistics label, reason PASS / FAIL and the deciding criterion label_stability share of bootstrap resamples (within speed levels) with the same verdict coverage the speed range and levels against the requirement

Coverage matters here. The test needs walking and running speeds. Commanded speeds must span at least 1.0 to 3.0 m/s with 8 speed levels (12 levels and 10 rollouts per level recommended). With fewer speeds the fit produces false PASS verdicts: in subsampled data, 68 % of draws with four speeds. Below the minimum the analysis is reported as not evaluable, not FAIL.

Joint torques must be the torques the actuators apply. For Isaac Lab's implicit PD actuators, the recorder takes them from PhysX (RL integration).

docs.title: Feedback signature: foot-placement control
docs.text:
Sensorimotor delays prevent purely continuous balance correction, so humans stabilize walking largely by stepping. Deviations of the body state during a step are corrected by where the next foot lands (Wang & Srinivasan 2014). How strongly, and how early in the stride, the pelvis state predicts the next foot placement is a signature of reactive feedback control.

Model (foot_placement): for each group (the unit of replication, e.g. one commanded speed of a simulation, or one human subject), at each of 101 phases of the stride: - the lateral placement of the swing foot at the next strike is regressed on the pelvis position and velocity at that phase; - this gives the phase-resolved gains (four pelvis-state coefficients) and the relative predictive power ΔR²(φ), the R² of the pelvis-state model minus that of a baseline using the swing foot's own state.

Both limbs are pooled per group, with right-limb strides mirrored.

Against the human reference (feedback, default camargo-treadmill/feedback): foot-placement fits of 21 adults walking overground (Camargo et al. 2021), with coordinate-based strikes.

Output Meaning fpgd, fpgd_mean foot-placement gain distance per group and its mean: at each phase, the Mahalanobis distance of the group's gains from the human gain distribution (covariance shrunk by 0.1 towards the identity), integrated over phases 1–100. Lower is closer peak_dr2, peak_timing the largest ΔR² of each group and the phase (%) at which it occurs comparison model vs human peak ΔR² and timing: means, difference, p-value, Cohen's d, the model mean's bootstrap interval fpgd_mean_ci 95 % bootstrap interval over groups coverage strides per group against the requirement (100 minimum, 250 recommended)

With few strides per group the fits are noisy and the FPGD is biased upward. Below 100 strides per group the analysis is reported as not evaluable (Data coverage).

docs.title: Feedforward signature: speed–stride relations
docs.text:
Humans do not choose stride length and stride frequency independently. Both rise with speed along a relation set before each step (Grieve 1966; Kuo 2001), which makes it a signature of feedforward control.

Per rollout (gait_summary): the mean speed, stride length and stride frequency over the strides after the transient (common definitions).

Against the human reference (gait_scaling, default camargo-treadmill/gait): each subject's mean stride length and frequency at each treadmill speed, 624 means of 22 adults at 0.50–2.05 m/s. Only the model rollouts within that speed range are compared.

Output Meaning js_stride_length, js_stride_frequency Jensen–Shannon divergence (bits; 0 identical, 1 disjoint) between the joint distributions of (speed, stride length) and (speed, stride frequency) of the model and the human data, from Gaussian kernel density estimates (Scott's rule) matched_stride_length, matched_stride_frequency at matched speed: the median robust z of the rollouts against the human median and spread at their speed, its interval, whether it lies within the human range, and the profile over speed (by_speed) *_ci 95 % bootstrap intervals over rollouts coverage speed levels covered against the requirement (3 minimum, 6 recommended)

The two measures answer different questions: - JS divergence compares whole distributions. It also reflects which speeds the data cover, and it saturates near 1 bit when the distributions do not overlap. - Matched-speed z compares each rollout with humans at its own speed. It does not depend on the speeds covered and does not saturate, and its sign says whether strides are too long or too short. When a model's deviation changes with speed, the median summarizes the speeds covered; by_speed shows the profile.

Other references can be passed with --gait-reference, for example a model's own training data.

docs.title: Foot strikes
docs.text:
A stride starts at a foot strike. There are two ways to find one:

  • Contact: the foot's vertical ground reaction force, low-pass filtered at 20 Hz, rises through 5 % of body weight. This is initial contact as clinical gait analysis defines it.
  • Kinematic: the data set's own strike marks, else the coordinate-based criterion of Zeni et al. (2008), the peak of the heel's anteroposterior distance ahead of the pelvis.

The two do not coincide. In human treadmill walking the kinematic event precedes contact by about 3 % of the stride. In simulated gaits it departs from contact by up to a quarter of the stride, because the models' leg motion differs from human leg motion.

docs.title: One rule
docs.text:
Each comparison uses the most accurate definition that both sides have. - Contact when the data set and the reference both have foot forces. - The kinematic event for both when either side has none.

Comparison Reference strides Data set with GRF Data set without GRF Feedforward (human treadmill data) contact (force plates) contact kinematic Feedback (human overground data) kinematic kinematic kinematic Sagittal angles (human treadmill data) contact contact kinematic Gait phases, kinetic principles contact contact (they analyse the forces) —

The decision is per data set. If any rollout lacks force data, every rollout uses the kinematic event, so a comparison never mixes the two. evaluate(..., strike_source="grf" | "provided" | "kinematic") forces one source for every analysis.

docs.title: Contact strikes in detail
docs.text:
A strike starts a contact of at least 0.1 s, at least 0.2 s after the previous strike. Two rules separate strikes from brief changes of load within a stance: - A reloading less than 30 % of the median swing after the end of the previous contact continues that stance. - So does a reloading within half the median stride of the previous strike.

In both cases the first contact is the strike. Brief touches (a foot tapping before it lands) are not strikes.

In very fast gaits every contact can be shorter than 0.1 s. For example, a robot stepping at 4–5 Hz has 0.09 s contacts and 0.22 s strides. When no stride is found, the minimum stance is scaled to 0.2 × the stride; human stance exceeds that even in sprinting.

docs.title: Stance and phases
docs.text: A foot's stance runs from its strike to the start of its swing, the longest interval of the stride without contact. Briefer unloadings (shorter than 30 % of that swing) belong to the stance. The phases of the stride are measured from both feet's stance.

docs.title: Phases of the stride
docs.text:
From both feet's stance at every sample (contact: vertical GRF above 5 % of body weight, 20 Hz low-pass; brief unloadings within a stance count as stance; Foot strikes), each stride of the left foot is divided into:

  • double support: both feet in stance;
  • single support: one foot;
  • flight: neither.
Output Meaning rollouts the mean fractions of each rollout's strides median medians over rollouts, and the share of rollouts with flight in more than 1 % of the stride, with bootstrap intervals

Human walking has double support (about 20–30 % of the stride at comfortable speeds) and no flight. The leaderboard row restricts both numbers to rollouts at walking speeds (0.9–1.5 m/s), where walking is expected.

docs.title: Kinetic principles
docs.text:
The ground reaction forces, joint powers and centre-of-mass mechanics are tested against six established principles of human walking. The principles are expressed as 16 predictions that can be checked in any model; the human reference (camargo-treadmill/kinetics) is evaluated with the same criteria.

Principle Predictions P1 step-to-step transition (Donelan et al. 2002; Kuo 2007) double support (fraction of stride); trailing-leg push-off work; leading-leg collision work; push-off + collision work rise with speed P2 ankle push-off (Winter 1983; Farris & Sawicki 2012) ankle share of positive joint work; ankle positive work rises with speed P3 joint roles (Winter 1983; DeVita et al. 2007; Sawicki et al. 2009) knee net work negative; ankle net work positive; hip net work positive P4 anteroposterior balance and propulsion (Turns et al. 2007; Nilsson & Thorstensson 1989) net AP impulse / propulsive impulse; peak propulsive force rises with speed P5 vertical GRF (Nilsson & Thorstensson 1989; Hebenstreit et al. 2015) double-humped vertical GRF; first peak rises with speed; stance fraction falls with speed P6 pendular energy exchange (Cavagna et al. 1976) energy recovery; recovery maximal at an intermediate speed

How each kind of prediction is tested. Each rollout is the mean over its strides of the reference foot within the human speed range (0.54–2.03 m/s).

  • magnitude: the robust z at matched speed; consistent when |median z| ≤ 2.
  • sign: the share of rollouts with the predicted sign; consistent when it is at least 0.8 × the human share.
  • direction (rises or falls with speed): the slope over speed; consistent when its 95 % bootstrap interval excludes zero in the predicted direction.
  • shape: a concave quadratic over speed with its vertex inside the range.

Direction and shape need rollouts spanning at least 0.6 m/s; with fewer speeds they are n/a.

Work, power and impulse are made dimensionless with body mass, gravity and leg length (Hof 1996) when subject.leg_length_m is given. Without sagittal joint moments the joint-work predictions (P2, P3) are n/a. Without a centre-of-mass signal the COM of each stride is integrated from the total GRF, as for the force-plate data of the human reference.

Output Meaning consistent, evaluated predictions consistent with human walking, and how many could be evaluated by_principle scores per principle predictions each prediction's value, interval, human value, consistent, Holm-corrected p coverage speed levels and rollouts per level against the recommendation (6 levels, 5 rollouts)

docs.title: Sagittal joint angles
docs.text:
Each rollout's mean gait cycle of the sagittal hip, knee and ankle angles is compared with human treadmill walking at the same speed. The leg is the one of dataset.sagittal_side; flexion and dorsiflexion are positive. The reference (camargo-treadmill/sagittal) holds the mean cycles of each of 22 subjects at each treadmill speed, 0.50–1.85 m/s.

Eight features of each rollout's cycle:

Feature Unit hip range of motion deg peak knee flexion deg timing of peak knee flexion % of the cycle knee loading flexion (early stance) deg knee angle at foot strike deg knee midstance minimum deg ankle range of motion deg timing of push-off plantarflexion % of the cycle

Each feature is compared with the human median and spread at the rollout's speed (robust z). It is consistent when the median z over rollouts lies within ±2. The shape distance compares the range-of-motion-normalized cycles with the mean human shape at the nearest speed, in % of the range.

Output Meaning features per feature: values, median difference, median z with its bootstrap interval, consistent consistent_features how many of the 8 are consistent, with a bootstrap interval shape_distance per joint, the median distance mean_cycle, speed the rollouts' mean cycle and speeds

A count near a threshold can flip between resamples. The interval of consistent_features and each feature's z interval show how firm it is.

docs.title: Adapters: motion capture and other sources
docs.text:
Every adapter produces the same signals of the profile (PROFILE.md); the analyses do not depend on where the data came from. Minari datasets with the profile need no adapter. The web app converts on the fly; humanlike convert writes the result as a Minari dataset with the profile, so that it can be shared and evaluated like any other. Positions are converted to metres; strides, speeds and gait cycles are then computed with one definition for every source (humanlike.gait).

humanlike convert <adapter> <input> mylab/name-v0 --name NAME [options]   # a Minari dataset
humanlike validate mylab/name-v0    # which analyses the data support, and why not the others
humanlike evaluate mylab/name-v0 -o results/
adapter input arrays it provides csv one CSV per rollout, or one CSV with a rollout column any profile signal, by column name c3d C3D motion capture (Vicon, Qualisys, Motion Analysis, ...) pelvis and feet from markers; foot GRFs from the force plates of an instrumented treadmill bvh BVH animation or motion-capture export pelvis and feet by forward kinematics mimickit MimicKit / Isaac Gym steering rollouts everything, at the physics rate curated the manuscript's curated rollouts pelvis, feet, foot strikes

docs.title: CSV
docs.text:
Columns are the profile signal names (PROFILE.md) with an axis or index suffix, for example time, pelvis_pos_x, pelvis_pos_y, pelvis_pos_z, left_foot_pos_x, ..., right_grf_z, sagittal_angles_hip, sagittal_angles_knee, sagittal_angles_ankle, joint_torque_0, .... pelvis_x, lfoot_x, rfoot_x (and left_foot_x, ...) are accepted for the core arrays. Without a time column give --fs; lengths in other units: --units mm. Other column names can be mapped in Python: convert(path, name, columns={"pelvis_pos": ["PX", "PY", "PZ"]}).

humanlike convert csv runs/ mylab/mypolicy-v0 --name MyPolicy --fs 50 --mass 70

docs.title: C3D
docs.text:
Each file is one rollout, grouped by the subject name stored in the file. Defaults follow Plug-in Gait: pelvis = mean of LASI, RASI, LPSI, RPSI (or SACR); feet = LHEE, RHEE. Gaps up to 0.1 s are filled and the longest complete stretch is kept. Foot strikes are taken at contact from the force plates where they cover the trial (instrumented treadmill), else detected from the markers (events="c3d" uses the file's Foot Strike events instead; see PROFILE.md, foot strikes).

humanlike convert c3d session/ mylab/s01-v0 --name S01                                  # over ground
humanlike convert c3d tm.c3d mylab/s01-tm-v0 --name S01 --treadmill-speed auto --mass 78   # treadmill

Treadmill trials are moved into over-ground coordinates by the belt travel (--treadmill-speed in m/s, or auto, estimated from the feet in stance), and their force plates give the GRF of each foot (each loaded plate assigned to the nearest foot). Over-ground force plates are left out because they cover a few steps only. Without centre-of-mass data the kinetic analysis integrates the GRF, as for the human reference. The reader (humanlike.adapters.c3d_reader) is plain numpy: Intel, DEC and MIPS files, integer and floating-point storage; markers, analog channels, forces and centres of pressure agree with ezc3d.

docs.title: BVH
docs.text:
The pelvis (Hips, Pelvis, ...) and feet (LeftFoot, LeftAnkle, ...) are found by name, ignoring prefixes such as mixamorig:; give pelvis=, left_foot=, right_foot= otherwise. BVH is usually y-up (default --up y); the unit is guessed from the pelvis height (--units auto) or given.

humanlike convert bvh clips/ mylab/clips-v0 --name Animation

docs.title: From Python
docs.text:
from humanlike.adapters import from_arrays          # any simulator: build the rollouts from arrays
from humanlike.adapters.c3d import convert
ds = convert("tm.c3d", "S01", treadmill_speed="auto", mass_kg=78)

docs.title: Humanlike locomotion profile 1.0
docs.text: The benchmark does not define a file format. It defines a profile: the signals a locomotion data set provides, their names, shapes, units and sign conventions, and the metadata the analyses need. The profile is carried by an existing community format, as BIDS conventions are carried by NIfTI, TSV and JSON files. The first mapping is Minari (Farama Foundation; HDF5 or Arrow), the dataset standard of Gymnasium-based reinforcement learning. Motion capture enters through the C3D, BVH and CSV adapters (ADAPTERS.md) and is converted to Minari datasets with the profile.

docs.title: Signals
docs.text:
Sampled at one rate fs per data set; positions in a right-handed world frame with the vertical axis up; the walking direction is found from the data.

signal shape unit required capability meaning pelvis_pos [T,3] m yes core pelvis (or root) position, a proxy of the centre of mass left_foot_pos [T,3] m yes core left foot position (ankle or foot body origin) right_foot_pos [T,3] m yes core right foot position pelvis_vel [T,3] m/s no core pelvis velocity; differentiated from pelvis_pos if absent joint_torque [T,J] N m no energetics actuated joint torques (generalized forces) joint_vel [T,J] rad/s no energetics matching joint velocities sagittal_angles [T,3] deg no sagittal hip, knee, ankle sagittal angles of one leg (dataset.sagittal_side), + = flexion / dorsiflexion left_grf [T,3] N no kinetics floor force on the left foot, world frame right_grf [T,3] N no kinetics floor force on the right foot, world frame com_pos [T,3] m no kinetics whole-body centre of mass; the pelvis is used if absent com_vel [T,3] m/s no kinetics centre-of-mass velocity; differentiated from com_pos if absent sagittal_moments [T,3] N m no joint_kinetics hip, knee, ankle sagittal joint moments of the sagittal_angles leg, + = flexion / dorsiflexion sagittal_powers [T,3] W no joint_kinetics matching joint powers; moment x angular velocity of sagittal_angles if absent left_heel_strike, right_heel_strike [T] bool no core foot-strike marks; used where the GRF does not cover the rollout

Conventions: ground reaction forces are the forces of the floor on the foot; sagittal angles, moments and powers are those of one leg (sagittal_side), positive for flexion / dorsiflexion; strides, speeds and gait cycles are computed by the package with one definition for every data set (humanlike.gait).

Foot strikes (humanlike.events.strikes, the events stage) follow one rule: each comparison uses the most accurate definition that both sides have. Contact is used when both the data set and the reference have foot forces; the kinematic event is used for both when either side has none. Every reference in the bundle states its definition (events in references/v1/manifest.json).

  • Contact. A foot's vertical GRF rising through 5 % of body weight (initial contact, Perry & Burnfield 2010). Brief reloadings within a stance are not strikes (humanlike.kinetics.foot_strikes).
  • Used with the human treadmill data, which have force plates: the feedforward comparison with them, the sagittal angles and the kinetics.
  • Used only when the GRF of every rollout covers it. The GRF covers a rollout when it gives at least half as many strikes as the kinematic criterion, so a force plate under a few overground steps does not.
  • Otherwise the whole data set uses the kinematic event, so a comparison never mixes the two.
  • A contact must last MIN_STANCE_S = 0.1 s to be a stance. In very fast gaits, where every contact is shorter, the minimum is scaled to 0.2 × the stride: robots that step at 4–5 Hz (Isaac Lab H1: 0.09 s contacts, 0.22 s strides) keep their strikes, while ordinary gaits and the manuscript models are unchanged.
  • Kinematic. The data set's own strike marks, else the coordinate-based criterion of Zeni et al. (2008). Used with the motion-capture references and the overground human data of the feedback signature, which have no forces at every stride, and for every data set without GRF.

The analyses of the forces themselves (gait phases, kinetic principles) delimit strides at contact. evaluate(..., strike_source="grf" | "provided" | "kinematic") forces one source for every analysis.

The rule exists because the two events differ. In human treadmill walking the coordinate-based event precedes contact by 3.4 % of the stride; in simulations it departs by up to a quarter of the stride (the manuscript's Supplementary Section on foot strikes). Stance runs from a strike to the start of the swing (the longest unloading of the stride), and the phases of the stride (double support, single support, flight) are measured from both feet's stance.

docs.title: Metadata
docs.text: key level required meaning fs data set yes rate of the profile signals (Hz) up data set no (default z) vertical axis mass_kg data set for energetics and kinetics body mass leg_length_m data set no hip joint centre to sole; dimensionless kinetics (Hof 1996) sagittal_side data set no (default left) leg of the sagittal signals; reference foot of the sagittal and kinetic analyses name, kind, simulator, skeleton data set no description joint_torque_source data set no how the joint torques were obtained when they are not the applied torques (e.g. an implicit PD drive's estimate) grf_source data set no how the ground reaction forces were obtained (e.g. normal forces only, without friction) group rollout no unit of replication of the feedback signature (session, subject) commanded_speed rollout no target speed (m/s) fell rollout no the agent fell; the rollout is excluded skip_s rollout no initial seconds to discard (start-up transient)

docs.title: What the data allow
docs.text: capability signals metadata analyses core pelvis_pos, left_foot_pos, right_foot_pos - events, gait_summary, gait_scaling, foot_placement, feedback energetics joint_torque, joint_vel subject.mass_kg energetics sagittal sagittal_angles - sagittal kinetics left_grf, right_grf subject.mass_kg gait_phases, kinetic_principles joint_kinetics sagittal_angles, sagittal_moments subject.mass_kg kinetic_principles (joint-work predictions)

docs.title: Minari mapping
docs.text:
profile Minari data set a Minari dataset (one model, or one group of human subjects) data-set metadata metadata.json → "humanlike_profile": {"profile": "humanlike-locomotion", "version": "1.0", "fs", "samples_per_step", "up", "mass_kg", ...} rollout an episode rollout metadata episode metadata: group, commanded_speed, fell, skip_s signals step infos: infos["humanlike"][signal], the samples_per_step samples recorded since the previous step, shape [k, ...]

The entry Minari stores at reset is not used, so an episode of n steps gives n × k samples. With k > 1 a control-rate environment can report physics-rate signals (for example 4 samples of 120 Hz ground reaction forces per 30 Hz step); fs is then k / control period.

docs.title: Recording rollouts
docs.text:
from humanlike.adapters.minari_io import collector, finish

class MyEnv(gym.Env):                      # or a wrapper around an existing environment
    def step(self, action):
        ...                                 # k physics substeps, recording the profile signals
        info["humanlike"] = {"pelvis_pos": pelvis[k_samples], "left_foot_pos": ..., "right_foot_pos": ...,
                             "left_grf": ..., "right_grf": ...}      # each [k, 3]
        return obs, reward, terminated, truncated, info
    # reset() returns the same keys and shapes in its info (the samples are not used)

env = collector(MyEnv())                    # minari.DataCollector with record_infos=True
...                                         # roll out the policy
finish(env, "mylab/mypolicy-v0", fs=120.0, samples_per_step=4, mass_kg=70.0, algorithm_name="...",
       episodes=[{"group": "speed_1.1", "commanded_speed": 1.1}, ...])   # adds the profile, checks the data

finish reads the dataset back and stops with the reason if a signal is missing; a dataset recorded without record_infos=True is reported with how to fix it. For an existing dataset, humanlike.adapters.minari_io.annotate(path, fs=..., samples_per_step=..., mass_kg=...) adds the metadata (no minari package needed).

humanlike validate mylab/mypolicy-v0        # a registered id or a dataset directory
humanlike evaluate mylab/mypolicy-v0 -o results/
humanlike convert c3d trial.c3d mylab/s01-v0 --name S01 --mass 70   # motion capture to Minari (ADAPTERS.md)

Reading and writing HDF5 datasets need only h5py (also in the browser); recording with DataCollector and writing Arrow need pip install "humanlike[minari]". Datasets written by humanlike convert, by humanlike.adapters.minari_io.write or by the web app's "Download the data as a Minari dataset" are for evaluation: they hold the core positions as observations and a zero action placeholder (marked "evaluation_only": true in the profile metadata), the profile signals are in the infos. They are written in the Minari 0.5 layout, compressed (gzip), and open with the minari package.

docs.title: Python API
docs.text: The main entry points; generated from their signatures and docstrings.

docs.title: humanlike.format.load
docs.text:
load(source) -> 'Dataset'

A data set from a Minari dataset with the humanlike profile (directory or registered id), or from the package's own container file (written by humanlike.format.write).

docs.title: humanlike.format.validate
docs.text:
validate(ds: 'Dataset') -> 'Report'

Check a data set against the profile (humanlike.format.spec): required metadata, array shapes and units, sampling rates, and which analyses (capabilities) its signals and metadata support. Errors make it invalid; warnings point at values to look at.

docs.title: humanlike.adapters.from_arrays
docs.text:
from_arrays(name: 'str', rollouts: 'list[dict]', *, mass_kg=None, leg_length_m=None, up='z', kind='simulation', simulator=None, skeleton=None, description=None, sagittal_side=None) -> 'Dataset'

rollouts: dicts with the rollout metadata (id, group, fs, and optionally commanded_speed, fell, skip_s) and an "arrays" dict named as in humanlike.format.spec.FIELDS.

docs.title: humanlike.adapters.minari_io.read
docs.text:
read(path_or_id, name: 'str | None' = None) -> 'Dataset'

A data set from a Minari dataset (directory, its data/ folder, or a registered id) that carries the humanlike profile metadata: the profile signals of every episode at their sampling rate, the episode metadata (group, commanded_speed, fell, skip_s, transient_dropped_s) and the dataset metadata. name overrides the dataset's name.

docs.title: humanlike.adapters.minari_io.write
docs.text:
write(ds: 'Dataset', dataset_id: 'str', *, samples_per_step: 'int' = 1, data_format: 'str' = 'hdf5', root=None, compress: 'bool' = True, author=None, algorithm_name=None, description=None, code_permalink=None) -> 'Path'

Write a data set as a Minari dataset with the profile, at //data (root: $MINARI_DATASETS_PATH or ~/.minari/datasets, as Minari). Returns the data directory.

HDF5 is written directly with h5py (the Minari layout, compressed with gzip and shuffle when compress), so neither minari nor its dependencies are needed, also in the browser; Arrow is written with the minari package. Observations are the core positions (pelvis, left foot, right foot) at the last sample of each step and actions a zero placeholder: such a dataset is for evaluation (marked evaluation_only), the profile signals are in the step infos.

docs.title: humanlike.adapters.minari_io.collector
docs.text:
collector(env, **kw)

minari.DataCollector for an environment whose step infos carry infos['humanlike'] (the infos are kept: record_infos=True).

docs.title: humanlike.adapters.minari_io.finish
docs.text:
finish(collector_env, dataset_id: 'str', *, fs: 'float', samples_per_step: 'int' = 1, episodes=None, check: 'bool' = True, mass_kg=None, leg_length_m=None, sagittal_side=None, up: 'str' = 'z', name=None, kind: 'str' = 'simulation', simulator=None, skeleton=None, joint_torque_source=None, grf_source=None, provenance=None, **minari_kw) -> 'Path'

Create the dataset from a DataCollector, add the profile metadata and (check) read it back, so that a missing signal is reported now rather than at evaluation. Returns the data directory.

docs.title: humanlike.adapters.minari_io.annotate
docs.text:
annotate(path_or_id, *, fs: 'float', samples_per_step: 'int' = 1, up: 'str' = 'z', mass_kg=None, leg_length_m=None, sagittal_side=None, name=None, kind='simulation', simulator=None, skeleton=None, episodes=None, evaluation_only: 'bool | None' = None, joint_torque_source=None, grf_source=None, provenance: 'dict | None' = None) -> 'Path'

Add the profile metadata to a Minari dataset (HDF5 or Arrow; the minari package is not needed); episodes: optional list of per-episode dicts (group, commanded_speed, fell, skip_s), in episode order. Returns the dataset's data directory.

docs.title: humanlike.engine.evaluate
docs.text:
evaluate(ds: 'Dataset', references: 'dict | None' = None, bundle: 'Bundle | None' = None, only=None, progress: 'Callable | None' = None, cache=None, **options) -> 'dict'

Run every applicable stage. Returns {"validation", "stages": {name: {status, title, reason, seconds, result, cached}}}; status is "ok", "skipped" or "error". cache: a humanlike.cache cache (MemoryCache, DirCache) or None.

docs.text:
row(res: 'dict') -> 'dict'

{column: value or None} plus "name", "signals" and "rollouts".

docs.text:
inspect(ds, strides: 'bool' = True) -> 'dict'

{dataset, subject, rollouts, signals, provenance, coverage}. strides: also count the foot-placement strides per group (the feedback signature's requirement; fits nothing, but detects the strides).

docs.title: humanlike.rl.evaluate_policy
docs.text:
evaluate_policy(make_env, policy, body_map, protocol_spec='locomotion-speed-v1', name: 'str' = 'policy', seed: 'int' = 0, evaluate: 'bool' = True, progress=None, check: 'bool' = True, recorder_kw: 'dict | None' = None, **evaluate_kw) -> 'dict'

Roll out the policy under the protocol, record the profile signals at the physics rate (HumanlikeRecorder) and run the analyses. Returns {"protocol", "dataset", "results", "check"}. With check, the first episode that did not fall is checked (humanlike.rl.checks) and a failure stops the run before the remaining rollouts are spent on a wrong body map or floor.

docs.title: humanlike.rl.conformance
docs.text:
conformance(ds, protocol_spec, checks: 'bool' = True)

Rows (name, "ok" | "fail" | "skip", message) of a humanlike.rl.checks.CheckReport: does the data set hold the protocol's rollouts? Falls are part of a model's result, so a fallen rollout counts towards its speed and may be shorter; every other rollout lasts the protocol's duration (one 30 Hz step of tolerance).

docs.title: humanlike.rl.recorder.HumanlikeRecorder
docs.text:
HumanlikeRecorder(env, body_map, model=None, data=None, info_key: 'str' = 'humanlike', fell_height: 'float | None' = 0.5, terminated_is_fall: 'bool' = True, physics_steps: 'int | None' = None, allow_env_rate: 'bool' = False, dtype=None, keep_transient: 'bool' = True, spill_dir=None)

Wraps a :class:gymnasium.Env to allow a modular transformation of the :meth:step and :meth:reset methods.

This class is the base class of all wrappers to change the behavior of the underlying environment. Wrappers that inherit from this class can modify the :attr:action_space, :attr:observation_space and :attr:metadata attributes, without changing the underlying environment's attributes. Moreover, the behavior of the :meth:step and :meth:reset methods can be changed by these wrappers.

Some attributes (:attr:spec, :attr:render_mode, :attr:np_random) will point back to the wrapper's environment (i.e. to the corresponding attributes of :attr:env).

Note: If you inherit from :class:Wrapper, don't forget to call super().__init__(env)

docs.title: Reference data
docs.text:
The analyses compare with human data from Camargo et al. (2021), A comprehensive, open-source dataset of lower limb biomechanics in multiple conditions of stairs, ramps, and level-ground ambulation and transitions, Journal of Biomechanics 119:110320. The data are licensed CC BY 4.0. The package ships derived summaries (references/v1):

Reference Content Used by camargo-treadmill/gait each subject's mean stride length and frequency at each treadmill speed (22 adults, 624 means, 0.50–2.05 m/s) feedforward camargo-treadmill/feedback foot-placement fits of each subject's overground walking (21 adults; coordinate-based strikes) feedback camargo-treadmill/sagittal each subject's mean sagittal hip, knee and ankle angles over the gait cycle at each treadmill speed (0.50–1.85 m/s) sagittal angles camargo-treadmill/kinetics per-stride GRF, joint-work and centre-of-mass features of the treadmill walking (18,873 strides, 0.5–2.05 m/s), with each subject's mass and leg length kinetic principles

Each reference states how its strides are delimited (events: contact or kinematic), and the analyses follow it (Foot strikes). humanlike references lists them. Other references with the same layout can be passed to evaluate (references={"gait": [...], ...}).

The motion-capture data the evaluated controllers were trained on (AMASS, the AMP reference motions, KIT) were used in the accompanying paper. They are not distributed, because their licences do not permit it.
